judgment.rationale: Both are Grade R (rank 0) Skills under the EMERGENT WRITING skill area. The second SFI sits in Term 2, Sub-strand Handwriting ('Traces simple outlines of pictures, patterns and own names where the correct starting point and writing direction are indicated on letters'); the first sits in the later Term 3, Sub-strand Emergent Writing ('Draws pictures to convey a message ... uses this as a starting point for writing. With help adds a word or phrase to a drawing'), with LCs 'Uses a drawing as a starting point for writing' and 'With help adds a word or phrase to a drawing'. Tracing letter shapes with correct starting point and writing direction is the handwriting control that supports the later, more independent production of an actual written word or phrase attached to a drawing, so the earlier-term handwriting skill plausibly supports success in the later-term emergent writing task; direction is therefore second_to_first, consistent with the Term 2 to Term 3 order within one grade. Note that the shared tokens 'starting point' and 'pictures' are used in different senses (stroke start/letter tracing versus drawing as a stimulus for writing), so lexical overlap alone was not treated as evidence; confidence is moderate because the dependency is partial (the drawing/message component does not require tracing). Both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and have truncated source and LC evidence, which limits full verification.

They are substantively coherent as reciprocal reader-writer audience skills: punctuating so others can read what was written is the writing-side counterpart of reading peers' and one's own writing, and classroom paired reading of peer texts gives the audience for punctuated writing. The evidence shows complementarity, not dependency: neither statement's proficiency is shown to condition success in the other, and both are in the same Grade and same Term, so no earlier-to-later developmental ordering is supported. judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Grade 3 (rank 3, resolved coordinates) Skills in the Writing skill area under the 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' sub-strand: the first (Term 2) requires use of more complex tenses (present and past progressive, e.g. 'He is reading a book'); the second (Term 3) requires identifying and using nouns, pronouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs and prepositions correctly, as reflected in its two Learning Components ('Identifies...' and 'Uses... correctly'). These are complementary grammar objectives that jointly support correct sentence grammar in written work, giving genuine pair-specific instructional coherence beyond generic CAPS repetition - so no_relation would understate the link. However, the Term 3 statement is not a deepening, extension or broadening of progressive-tense control; it is a different grammar topic (metalinguistic word-class knowledge) that merely lists 'verbs' among six classes, and nothing in the bounded evidence shows that tense proficiency materially raises the likelihood of success at word-class identification and usage. Any dependency reading arguably runs from word-class knowledge toward verb-form control, which within one Grade would be an invalid Term 3 -> Term 2 direction; that ambiguity further rules out buildsTowards. The nomination signals (shared Grade ancestor, rank gap 0, Jaccard ~0.065 on 'and'/'uses', one shared LC tag 'grammar') are weak and non-semantic and cannot license development. Canonical symmetric relatesTo with null direction is therefore the correct complete judgment. Evidence limitations: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all endpoints and ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context (including merged Grade 3 and Term banner nodes), so this rests on the bounded statement text, LCs and placement.

'Reads as a whole class with teacher big books or other enlarged texts' specifies the shared-reading participation format, while 'Identifies the sequence of events in what was read' specifies a comprehension response to the text read in that setting (LC tags comprehension/events/reading/sequence). Canonical symmetric relatesTo with null direction is therefore the complete judgment. judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade R (rank 0), Term 2, Skill Area 'Emergent Reading', but under different sub-strands: the second under 'Emergent reading skills' and the first under 'Independent Reading'. The second specifies the enabling emergent-reading behaviours — using pictures to predict the story, 'reading' picture and caption books while understanding that pictures and words are related but different, and pointing to words when 'reading' (LCs: picture books/prediction; pointing/tracking/words). The first requires the child to apply those same pretend-reading behaviours autonomously and for pleasure with self-chosen books in the library or reading corner. Competence in picture-based meaning-making and word-pointing substantively supports success in sustained independent book handling and 'reading', so the support runs second to first; the reverse is not evidenced. Same-grade/same-term placement makes this direction permissible, and the judgment rests on the pair-specific capability difference (enabling strategy vs. independent application) rather than shared ancestors, page proximity or the generic 'books/reading' token overlap. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated and the first endpoint's LC evidence is truncated, so this is an inferred, moderately confident reading of the bounded excerpts.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Grade R (rank 0) Skills concerning visual processing of letters and shapes in emergent literacy. The first (Term 4, Listening and Speaking (Oral) / 'Uses visual and pictorial cues to make meaning') requires distinguishing the shapes of different letters and words and sorting plastic letters into same-letter groups (LC tags: letters, shapes, sorting, visual discrimination). The second (Term 1, Emergent Reading / 'Emergent reading skills') requires using memory skills to recall items seen such as letters, shapes or concrete objects (LC tags: emergent reading, memory, recall, visual memory). These are complementary visual-perceptual capabilities operating on the same curricular objects, giving meaningful, pair-specific instructional coherence beyond generic repetition or shared wording. However, recall of seen items and discrimination/sorting of letter forms are distinct skills in different Skill Areas and sub-strands; neither statement is a substantive extension, combination or increased-complexity version of the other, and the evidence does not show that proficiency in one makes success in the other more likely, so no developmental dependency (in either direction) is warranted. Nomination signals are hierarchy proximity (shared Grade R ancestor, rank gap 0) and weak lexical overlap ('letters', 'shapes', 'visual'; jaccard ~0.07-0.11), which are not semantic verdicts. Limitations: source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each) and both endpoints and all ancestors carry upstream audit/merge/code context, including merged Grade R and Term banner nodes, so this judgment rests on the printed statement text, Term/Skill Area scope and supplied LC metadata.

Direction is within the same Grade and same Term, which is permitted, and the gap in capability (muscle readiness vs. producing letter-based written forms) is substantive rather than generic. judgment.rationale: First endpoint: Grade 3 (rank 3), Term 1, Reading and Phonics, Phonics sub-strand - 'Recognises that some sounds are represented by a number of different spelling choices (play, pain, plate; feet, read, key; ...)'. Second endpoint: Grade 3 (rank 3), Term 4, Writing, 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' sub-strand - 'Drafts, writes, edits and publishes own story of at least two paragraphs (at least 12 sentences)', with Learning Components separating drafting, writing, editing and publishing. There is real, pair-specific instructional coherence: awareness that one sound has several grapheme options is orthographic knowledge a learner draws on when spelling and when editing a self-written text, so the two statements reinforce each other across the Reading/Phonics and Writing strands. But the evidence does not show the phonics recognition skill being extended, deepened or combined into the target: the target is defined by extended narrative composition and the full draft-to-publication process, a capability developed in the Writing strand rather than grown out of this recognition bullet, and CAPS presents the two strands in parallel within Grade 3. The nomination signals (shared Grade banner ancestor only, single shared token 'of', weak same-rank proximity, incidental trigrams) carry no semantic weight. Symmetric relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment rather than a developmental buildsTowards claim. Material limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), and all endpoints and ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context that was inspected (Grade 3 and Term banners are merged banner nodes; the sub-strand headings are singletons), so full source wording could not be verified.

Evidence limits noted: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and endpoints/ancestors carry upstream merge/audit context, so the judgment rests on the printed statement text, identity scope (Grade 3, Term 1/Term 2, Reading and Phonics, Phonics) and LC tags (spelling/phonics/sight words vs homophones/phonics/word meaning).

A first_to_second buildsTowards would run from Term 3 back to Term 1 within the same grade and is therefore invalid; the permitted second_to_first direction (contributing drawn ideas to a news book enabling hand-muscle strengthening activities) is not supported by the statement content, since the motor-development bullet does not depend on prior idea contribution. relatesTo is the supported judgment. Note both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all ancestors carry upstream merge/audit context, so only the supplied bullet text and identity scopes were used.

The source refs place them as sibling bullets in the same Grade 3 Term 1 Reading and Phonics table (rows 4 and 3 of segment 29f33b4e..., window 43), i.e. concurrently scheduled components of one term's reading programme. Control of joined letter formation within short words supports success in that broader, paced completion of the whole cursive alphabet, so proficiency in the Term 3 statement supports the Term 4 statement. Shared LC tags (copying, cursive, handwriting, writing) and wording overlap corroborate but do not alone drive this judgment. judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit under the same Grade 3, Term 2, Reading and Phonics / 'Phonic Activities three times a week for 15 minutes' sub-strand (same rank 3, same term), so shared placement alone is not decisive. The pair-specific evidence is a component-to-application relationship: the first SFI is a narrow decoding/recognition item ('Recognises digraphs making /f/ (e.g. ph as in elephant, gh as in laugh)', LC tags digraphs/phonics/sounds), while the second applies phonic knowledge productively and more broadly ('Spells words correctly using phonic knowledge in informal tests, in dictation and in all written work', LC tags dictation/phonic knowledge/spelling/written work). Knowing that particular sounds can be represented by different letter patterns such as 'ph'/'gh' supports the likelihood of success in spelling words correctly from phonic knowledge in dictation and written work, which is the wider, more independent application. Direction is first_to_second within the same Grade and Term, which is permitted; this is an inferred curriculum-grounded relation, and both endpoints' source evidence (and the second endpoint's LC evidence) is truncated, so the judgment rests on the bounded statement text and shared Phonics placement.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs sit in Grade R (rank 0), Listening and Speaking (Oral), sub-strand 'Uses visual and pictorial cues to make meaning', so direction is determined by Term within the grade. The first SFI is Term 2 and operationalises 'distinguishes between the shape of different letters and words' through general visual-discrimination activities (sorting identical objects, picking the odd picture out of a near-identical sequence and explaining why). The second SFI is Term 4 and applies the same discrimination to print itself: sorting plastic letters into groups of the same letter. That is a pair-specific shift from generic object/picture discrimination to letter-specific matching and categorisation, so Term 2 proficiency plausibly supports success in the Term 4 statement; the Term 2 to Term 4 direction is the permitted earlier-to-later order within Grade R. Shared LC tags (visual discrimination, sorting, shapes) and wording overlap alone were not treated as sufficient; the change in the sorted material carries the judgment. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all nodes carry upstream audit/merge context, so the full printed term context was not inspectable.
